claims.text: Molecular dynamics simulations using interatomic potentials can investigate the atomic-scale thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
State-of-the-art interatomic potentials tailored for HEA systems are available for the proposed FeCuCrCoNi simulations.
The initial FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles are as-synthesized solid solutions.
The relevant FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticle sizes extend from below 10 nm upward.
Heating simulations over temperatures below and above the thermal transitions can reveal structural and chemical evolution in HEA nanoparticles.
The thermal stability and melting behavior of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles depend on nanoparticle size.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have lower effective melting points than larger ones.
Elevated temperatures produce pronounced atomic diffusion in FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles may undergo surface phase separation during heating.
Smaller nanoparticles have higher surface-to-volume ratios than larger nanoparticles.
A higher surface-to-volume ratio increases atomic mobility and diffusion at elevated temperatures.
Enhanced atomic diffusion can drive surface phase separation and surface-layer melting in HEA nanoparticles.
Enhanced surface-mediated mobility reduces the thermal stability of smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles relative to larger ones.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles will exhibit structural changes, including surface melting or phase separation, at lower temperatures than larger particles.
Larger FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles will show more bulk-like behavior and higher thermal stability.
The accuracy of the predicted thermal response depends on the fidelity of the interatomic potential and its representation of alloy disorder.
Oxidation, supports, and experimental defects may modify the practical thermal behavior relative to the simulated behavior.
